title: 2026 Science Nobel Prizes Honor a Light Switch for the Brain, Ghostly Particles and Mirror-Image Molecules
summary:
Every year, two groups in Stockholm, Sweden, announce the Nobel Prizes in science, some of the most respected awards on Earth. The 2026 prizes went to work in biology, physics and chemistry.

The physics prize went to the man behind the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole. IceCube led to the discovery of neutrinos, tiny ghostly particles, coming from beyond our solar system. The chemistry prize honored work on making certain handed molecules. Like your left and right hands, these molecules are mirror images of each other.

The prize in physiology or medicine went to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. They developed a way to control nerve cells with light, called optogenetics.

The human brain has nearly 90 billion neurons, or nerve cells. They connect through about 100 trillion links. Scientists had long hoped for a tool to turn specific neurons on or off with great precision.

The story began with a tiny green alga, a living thing made of just one cell. In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel, who worked in Germany, studied a protein in the alga's eye spot called channelrhodopsin. When light hits this protein, it opens like a tiny gate and lets charged particles flow into the cell. That creates an electrical signal.

Deisseroth, a neuroscientist at Stanford University in California, was part of a team that put the gene for this protein into nerve cells. When they shined light on the cells, the cells reacted right away. In mice, the team used blue light to control whisker movements.

Optogenetics changed brain science. Researchers say it could help them find treatments for conditions such as blindness, depression and dementia.
why_it_matters: These prizes show how curiosity about simple things, like an alga's eye spot or tiny particles from space, can open new ways to understand the brain and the universe.

background_read: The Nobel Prizes are famous international awards, and each year the science prizes honor discoveries in physics, chemistry, and physiology or medicine.
The winners are chosen by expert groups in Stockholm, Sweden, and the prizes often go to work done years earlier that later proved very important.
Neurons in the brain communicate using tiny electrical signals, so a tool that can start those signals on command lets scientists test what each brain circuit does.
Optogenetics grew from basic research on a single-celled green alga, showing how studying simple living things can lead to big advances.
